concepts.title: The Mummy Meets Modern Science: The CT Scan
concepts.definition: More than three millennia after his death, the boy king Tutankhamun is wheeled from his tomb in the Valley of the Kings into a computed tomography scanner. The saga that began with Howard Carter's discovery continues through a CT scan that images the mummy layer by layer without disturbing a single binding.
concepts.key_idea: From candle-lit tomb to digital slices -- archaeology hands the boy king to machine vision, and the saga continues.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehb103.txt opening and scan sections (forensic reconstruction, computed tomography, mummy taken for scanning, valley of the kings)

solution_steps.explain: The mummy is moved briefly from its resting place so a portable CT unit can record hundreds of cross-sectional images.
The scan seeks the truth of the king's life and death -- age, health, and the cause that ended him -- without unwrapping damage.
Each era re-examines Tut with its best tools -- Carter's chisels, X-rays, now computed tomography -- the saga continuing across generations.

concepts.title: Carter's Discovery and the Buried Treasure
concepts.definition: Howard Carter's 1922 breakthrough opened a tomb stuffed with funerary treasures -- golden coffins, jewellery, ritual objects -- made for a king's afterlife. But Carter's eager clearing did its own harm: hot knives and resins cemented the body to the coffin, and the mummy was cut apart and reassembled in modern sand, bone by bone.
concepts.key_idea: Treasure found, mummy damaged -- the first discovery's haste taught later science what not to do.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehb103.txt carter sections (howard carter 1922, funerary treasures, resins, cutting the body free, burglar evidence of ancient robbery)

solution_steps.explain: After years of searching, Carter cleared the tomb of Tutankhamun and revealed astonishing golden furnishings.
Ritual resins had hardened like cement; to free the body, Carter's team heated knives and prised the limbs apart, leaving the mummy in pieces.
What treasure-hunting tolerated, today's archaeology forbids -- the difference underlines the chapter's theme of improving inquiry.

concepts.title: Findings of the Scan: A Family History and a Broken Body
concepts.definition: The scan and later research sketch Tut's life: a boy king of a powerful dynasty descending from Amenhotep III and Akhenaten, the heretic who promoted the worship of Aten; a body with a broken sternum and bent foot; and an early death whose exact cause remains debated -- illness, accident or foul play.
concepts.key_idea: Bones testify -- a dynasty's story, a heretic's revolution, and a boy's mysterious end read from a scanned skeleton.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehb103.txt findings sections (amenhotep akhenaten aten worship, broken body, sternum, foot, mystery of death, speculated causes)

solution_steps.explain: The chapter places Tut in the line of Amenhotep III and Akhenaten, whose radical shift to worshipping the Aten disrupted Egypt's old gods.
Imaging shows a cleft palate, a bent left foot, and damage near the chest -- clues debated as disease, accident or post-mortem breakage.
Science narrows but does not close the case; the chapter's point is the honest, ongoing questioning.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Compare Carter's examination of the mummy with the modern CT scan in terms of method and damage.

solution_template.explain: Carter's team used heat and leverage to strip the body from its coffin, breaking it apart.
The CT scanner images layer upon layer without touching a single binding or bone.
Inquiry has moved from extraction to observation -- gaining answers while preserving the evidence.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Why does the chapter call Tut's death an unfinished mystery? Present the competing explanations it mentions.

solution_template.explain: Illness or a bad leg, an accident such as a fall or chariot mishap, and possible foul play by rivals all circulate.
The scan documents body damage but cannot certify which event killed the young king.
Hence the saga continues -- each new technique refines the questions even where it cannot settle the verdict.
